results.title: Dippr: A data platform served to your agents, with one prompt | Product Hunt
results.content:
We’ve spent years working on data infrastructure, and this is the first time we’ve seen the person who needs the answer also be the person who can build the tool. Dippr is our bet on what the data platform looks like when that’s true: query your data where it lives, give agents only the access their user has, keep one definition of every metric, and host whatever gets built.  
  
If your team is already letting agents touch company data, tell us how you’re doing it today and where it breaks. [...] The agents could build almost anything, but they couldn't reach the data safely. Someone on support needed numbers from our warehouse they didn't have access to, and we wanted to say yes without handing over the keys to the whole warehouse. Everyone was building, but the numbers didn't match from one tool to the next, which caused confusion. And whatever they built stayed local and static. Only a few lucky ones ever got hosted. [...] So we built Dippr, a complete data platform reimagined for agents, served to them with one prompt.  
  
- Dippr connects to all your sources and tools, and agents query across them at once, on our own federated query engine.  
  
- You set permissions per agent, even when the person using it has no login to the source, so each agent sees only what it should.

results.title: Why AI Agents Fail in Production - by Paolo Perrone
results.content:
Three months later, your engineering team has burned $500K on a pilot that’s sitting on a shelf. The agent works fine on Tuesdays when the API is responsive, the user says exactly what the system prompt expects, and nothing in the database has changed. It falls apart everywhere else.

The LLM isn’t the problem. The LLM worked in the demo, and it works now. The problem is everything the demo didn’t show you.

## TL;DR [...] 2. Authentication rot. OAuth tokens expire. API keys rotate. Service accounts get locked. An agent that worked at 10am is broken by 2pm because a token refreshed. The automated renewal process fails silently. Nobody notices until users report errors. On May 1, 2025, LangSmith’s SSL certificate expired after its automated renewal had been silently failing since January. The culprit: a conflicting DNS record from a dangling Terraform config. For 28 minutes, 55% of API requests to the platform [...] Gartner predicts 40%+ of agentic AI projects will be scrapped by 2027. Not because the models fail. Because the systems around them weren’t engineered for production.
 Three failure patterns account for most of it: Dumb RAG (bad context management), Brittle Connectors (broken tool integrations), and the Compounding Error problem (mistakes that multiply across steps).

results.title: AI agents aren't confidently wrong because of bad context — they're wrong because of bad data engineering | VentureBeat
results.content:
Blaming the model: The first instinct is to blame the model, try a different LLM, adjust the prompt. The real problem lies further upstream, at the data engineering layer, the same instinct behind the fintech failure above: monitoring built for the pipeline, not the data. [...] # AI agents aren't confidently wrong because of bad context — they're wrong because of bad data engineering

You spend weeks tuning an AI chatbot. Answers are accurate. Stakeholders sign off, and you ship it. Three months later, the system is confidently wrong about a third of what users ask. Nobody changed the model, and nobody touched the prompts. The world moved, pricing changed, a policy updated, a product spec shipped a new version, and the underlying knowledge store didn't move with it. [...] If you can't answer those questions, then the gap lies in the pipeline between your source systems and whatever your agent reads from. That’s a data engineering fix, not a model swap or a vendor migration.

Whether you're building reporting pipelines, ML systems, or AI agents, correctness, freshness, consistency, and lineage are what make data trustworthy. AI simply exposes weaknesses that have existed in data engineering all along.

results.title: Build Agents, Automate Workflows, and Unlock Your Content—All in One Platform - Egnyte Blog
results.content: New conditional logic brings additional power to workflows, and now, agents can be part of the flow as well. Any agent in your library can be invoked directly inside a workflow, or you can run a prompt against your content. For example, a project manager uploads a submittal. A workflow fires instantly, extracting metadata, routing by trade type, flagging spec conflicts, triggering approval, and filing the result automatically. What used to take two days of email chains and multiple manual [...] Most AI initiatives that involve agents stall because building effective agents has looked like a developer’s job. All-new Agent Builder changes that: Describe what you need in plain English and go. Pick your data sources, wire up recommended connectors, and configure everything through an easy-to-follow setup that anyone can tackle. The person who knows the workflow builds the agent. No explaining it to engineering. [...] Most enterprise content sits idle. More than 80% of it is unstructured: Your contracts, submittals, financial reports, and scanned forms have no metadata AI can use to find, filter, or act on them at scale. AI can read any one of those documents. It can't work across fifty thousand of them. The traditional fix is manual tagging, and it doesn't scale—it's slow, inconsistent, and every untagged file widens the gaps in audit readiness, AI accuracy, and governance.
